study.title: 1 Kings 5 Preparation for the construction of the temple and the covenant with Hiram
study.overview: This chapter shows Solomon consolidating a peaceful relationship with Hiram, king of Tyre, to obtain wood and skilled labor for the construction of the house of the LORD. The text emphasizes that the work is born from the rest granted by God, from the fulfillment of the promise made to David and the careful organization of human and material resources. At the same time, the narrative already anticipates the cost of the great work: international cooperation, fair payment, but also call for compulsory work in Israel.

outline.title: Solomon asks for help building the house of the LORD
outline.explanation: Hiram, who was already a friend of David, congratulates Solomon; the king of Israel explains that the peace received from God enables him to build the temple and ask for cedares from Lebanon and skilled workers.

outline.title: Hirão agrees and the alliance is confirmed
outline.explanation: Hiram recognizes the wisdom given by God to Solomon, commits himself to supplying wood and receives food in return for his house; the text summarizes the peace between them and attributes the wisdom of Solomon to the LORD.

outline.title: Organization of labor and preparation of materials
outline.explanation: Solomon recruits workers from Israel, distributes shifts and supervision, has brought large stones and wood, and the artisans of Solomon and Hiram prepare everything for construction.

study.context: The chapter takes place at the beginning of Solomon's reign, when he seeks partners for the work of the temple. The text mentions Sidom, Tyre and Lebanon only as references related to the supply of wood and technical knowledge of the workers, without detailing more than that. The narrative also shows a common practice of large-scale job recruitment for large real projects.
study.theology: The theological center of the chapter is God's initiative: the rest of Solomon, the wisdom granted to him and the possibility of building the house to the name of the LORD are presented as divine gifts, not as mere political capacity. The construction of the temple appears as the fulfillment of the word given to David, showing continuity between promise and fulfillment. The use of the expression "the name of the LORD" highlights that the temple is not only a building, but a place dedicated to the public honor of the character and presence of the God of Israel. At the same time, the chapter also suggests that sacred works require planning, cooperation and justice in human relations, although the narrative maintains in tension this order with the weight of tribute and forced labor.

scholarViews.insight: King Hiram appears as David's former ally and a possible alliance partner; the relationship with Solomon continues this political and commercial friendship.
The delivery of the wood by Hiram and the sending of wheat by Solomon show the mutual fulfillment of the agreement and the importance of justice in the transactions between them.
The observation about the "stonemakers" highlights that the term can refer to the inhabitants of Gebal, recognized for their technical skill, and not just simple stone cutters.

questions: What does the chapter teach about the relationship between the peace received from God and the accomplishment of a work for his honor?
How does the cooperation between Solomon and Hiram combine practical wisdom, commitment and responsibility before God?
How to carefully read the presence of compulsory work in the chapter without losing focus on building the temple?
study.practice: Take a time to examine which designs of your life have been guided more by haste or prestige than by rest, wisdom, and obedience. Then seek to act with planning, just partnerships and clear spiritual purpose. If you lead something in the church, in the home or at work, think about how to honor God also in the way of organizing people, resources and deadlines.
study.uncertainty: The text provided does not describe in detail the geography, the exact date or the political extension of the agreements, so this information should not be expanded beyond what the chapter and the notes support. It is also not possible to state with certainty, from the notes, all the details of foreign workers and Israelis beyond what has been explicitly said.
